assumptions: Many conditions with unknown heterogeneous patterns of differential expression
conclusion: Multi-condition analysis needs to learn shared effect patterns while directly modeling counts because Poisson standard errors do not naturally support mash and log transformations can bias LFC estimates.
scope: Motivation for joint count modeling, especially with small or zero counts.
span: However, there is no straightforward way to integrate a Poisson model with mash because the Poisson model does not naturally provide summary statistics — effect estimates and standard errors — that can be used by mash; in particular, estimates of standard errors are unreliable in Poisson models (Robinson and Smyth,, 2008). An alternative would be to combine mash with a Gaussian measurement model for log-transformed scRNA-seq counts (Finak et al.,, 2015, e.g.,). However, as has been repeatedly pointed out (Lun,, 2018; Townes et al.,, 2019; Crowell et al.,, 2020, e.g.,), this data transformation can lead to severe bias in the LFC estimates.

objects: CorMotif; shared patterns of differential expression
assumptions: CorMotif compares two groups across independent studies; Poisson mash compares conditions
conclusion: CorMotif and Poisson mash share the idea of borrowing shared DE patterns for detection, while CorMotif does not directly model counts or estimate LFC effects.
scope: Shared strategy with different analysis setup and targets.
span: Additionally, in contrast with Poisson mash, CorMotif focuses on DE detection, and not on estimation of the effect sizes (log-fold changes), and CorMotif does not directly model the counts. Despite these differences, CorMotif shares with Poisson mash the idea of modeling shared patterns of DE across multiple studies (they call these patterns “correlation motifs”), and using these shared patterns to increase power of DE detection.

objects: lfsr; sparse LFC patterns; data-driven rank-one covariance matrices
assumptions: Simulated effects sparse across conditions and fitted data-driven rank-one prior covariances
conclusion: In sparse-effect simulations, mash and Poisson mash RUV underestimated lfsr, mainly attributed to data-driven rank-one covariance matrices.
scope: Observed calibration failure in the stated simulation setting, not a universal theorem.
span: Our simulations showed that when true the LFCs were sparse among conditions (i.e., non-null genes are differentially expressed in only a small subset of conditions, corresponding to sparse covariance matrices \bm{U}_{k} 𝑼k\bm{U}_{k}), the lfsr was underestimated by both mash and Poisson mash RUV. We found that this was mostly due to the use of data-driven rank-1 covariance matrices in the mash prior (Urbut et al.,, 2019).

assumptions: Cells are aggregated by condition before analysis
conclusion: Pseudobulk aggregation loses information and prevents capture of more complex patterns of differential expression between conditions.
span: We took a “pseudobulk” approach that aggregates cells by condition before performing the DE analysis. This aggregation step inevitably leads to a loss of information, preventing us from capturing more complex patterns of DE between conditions (Zhang et al.,, 2022).

conclusion: The current formulation assumes one replicate per condition, and condition-specific random effects provide only an imperfect replacement for within-condition replicates.

span: Another limitation of our current implementation is that it assumes one replicate per condition. Incorporation of condition-specific random effects, \bm{\eta}_{j} 𝜼j\bm{\eta}_{j}, into our model softens this limitation, essentially by using variability across conditions to serve as an imperfect replacement for within-condition replicates.
